blocks.text: 1. Real-Time Prediction
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444356724-890688201.png

Batch Prediction, the previous topic, accepted a genuine staleness tradeoff, predictions only as fresh as the last scheduled run. Real-Time Prediction serves a single request immediately instead, the moment it actually arrives, with no waiting for any next scheduled run at all.

An answer is expected within milliseconds, and the underlying Inference Pipeline, the same bundled preprocessing-plus-model object covered in its own topic, runs on one single row at a time, sitting behind an always-on serving server rather than a scheduled batch job.
2. The Request Flow
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444356724-707218008.png

A client sends one single request, an HTTP call carrying a single row of features for instance, which an always-on serving server receives and processes immediately. The already-loaded Inference Pipeline, kept ready in memory rather than loaded fresh for each request, runs pipeline.predict on this one row.

The resulting prediction is returned directly in the HTTP response, and the total round-trip time, from request sent to response received, is typically tens to low hundreds of milliseconds for a well-built real-time serving system, a dramatically different time scale from a batch job's hours-long run.
3. Always-On Infrastructure
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444356724-236415080.png

This connects directly back to Batch Prediction's compute-that-shuts-down infrastructure pattern. Real-Time Prediction instead needs a server running continuously, ready to handle any incoming request at any moment, since there is no predictable schedule to wait for.

The Inference Pipeline itself is loaded into memory once when the server starts, then kept ready there rather than reloaded fresh for every single incoming request, since reloading a serialized file from disk on every request would add unacceptable latency. This produces a genuinely different cost profile than batch prediction: paying continuously for standby readiness, not merely for the compute actually used during a scheduled run.

blocks.title: warn
blocks.content: Loading the Inference Pipeline fresh from disk on every single incoming request, rather than once at server startup, is a common early mistake that quietly destroys real-time latency. Load once, keep it resident in memory, and reuse it across every request.

blocks.text: 4. Where the Latency Budget Goes
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444356725-643988750.png

The latency in a real-time request is spent across several distinct stages. The network round trip accounts for the time the request and response actually spend traveling between client and server, entirely outside the model's own control.

Preprocessing accounts for time spent running the pipeline's imputation, encoding, and scaling steps, and model inference itself accounts for the actual prediction computation. When speed genuinely matters, every single millisecond across this entire budget gets scrutinized, since a slow preprocessing step can dominate total latency just as easily as a slow model can.

blocks.text: 5. The Scaling Challenge
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444356725-253617864.png

A genuine challenge unique to real-time serving is that request volume can spike unpredictably, a flash sale or a sudden viral event driving far more traffic than any typical day. A single server handling all of this traffic alone can quickly become overwhelmed, causing slow or outright failed responses precisely when demand, and business value, is highest.

The standard solution is running multiple identical serving instances behind a load balancer, so traffic spreads automatically across every available instance, scaling the number of running instances up or down as demand actually changes, rather than relying on any single server to absorb unpredictable spikes alone.
6. Timeouts and Fallback Behavior
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444356725-982714549.png

What happens when a real-time prediction takes too long, or fails outright, matters just as much as the happy path itself. Setting an explicit timeout means the system fails fast rather than leaving a caller waiting indefinitely for a response that may never arrive.

Defining a clear fallback behavior for that failure case, returning a safe default value, or a cached previous prediction for that same entity, keeps the overall system usable even when the model itself cannot respond in time, rather than letting one slow prediction cascade into a broader outage for whatever feature depends on it.

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: A well-designed real-time serving system treats "the model is temporarily unavailable" as an expected, planned-for case, not a surprise, since network issues, resource contention, and traffic spikes are all a normal part of running any live service.

blocks.text: 7. The Accuracy Versus Speed Tradeoff
https://algorithmxlr8-content-media.s3.ap-south-1.amazonaws.com/diagrams/1785444503134-112995675.png

This connects back to Ensemble Learning's large models, hundreds of boosted trees for instance, already covered in that module. A larger, more accurate model often takes meaningfully longer to run per individual prediction, simply because there is more computation involved in producing each answer.

Real-Time Prediction forces a direct, explicit tradeoff between accuracy and response speed that batch prediction largely avoids. A batch job, without the same tight time pressure bearing down on every single row, can more freely use the largest, most accurate model available, while a real-time system may need to accept a smaller, faster, slightly less accurate model specifically to stay within its latency budget.
8. Connecting to Monitoring

This connects forward to Monitoring, an upcoming topic later in this Model Deployment module. A real-time server must track latency and error rate continuously, on every single request, not just periodically, since real-time serving problems manifest immediately rather than being caught at the next scheduled check.

A slow or failing serving endpoint affects live users immediately, unlike a delayed batch job whose failure might only be noticed the next morning. This immediacy makes continuous, real-time monitoring of the serving endpoint itself a genuinely essential companion to Real-Time Prediction, not an optional extra.
9. When Real-Time Prediction Is the Right Choice

Real-Time Prediction is the right choice for fraud detection on a transaction as it actually happens, where staleness is genuinely unacceptable, and for any live, user-facing feature, a search ranking or a chat response for instance, where a user is actively waiting for an immediate answer.

For scoring a large volume of data with no genuine urgency behind it, Batch Prediction, covered in the previous topic, remains the better, more cost-efficient choice instead, since paying for always-on infrastructure when nothing is actually time-sensitive is simply unnecessary overhead.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

items: Real-Time Prediction serves a single request immediately, running the Inference Pipeline on one row behind an always-on server.
A client request reaches the server, the preloaded pipeline predicts, and the response returns within milliseconds.
Real-time serving needs a continuously running server with the pipeline preloaded, a different cost profile than batch.
Latency is spent across network round trip, preprocessing, and model inference, each worth scrutinizing.
Unpredictable traffic spikes are handled by running multiple instances behind a load balancer.
Explicit timeouts and defined fallback behavior keep the system usable when a prediction is slow or fails.
Real-time serving forces an explicit accuracy-versus-speed tradeoff that batch prediction largely avoids.
A real-time server needs continuous latency and error-rate tracking, connecting to the Monitoring topic later in this module.
Next up: Monitoring, tracking a deployed model's health and performance continuously once it is live.
